intro: Leesburg's big trees are measured, not legendary. Loudoun County remeasured its Big Tree Registry in 2025, and four of its trees stand within a hundred metres of each other on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Church in the old town. Among them are a silver linden 6.25 metres round and an Atlantic white cedar, both Virginia champions, and a Japanese chestnut the experts took a while to name. Beyond them are a white oak the town says is older than Leesburg itself, a tulip tree nearly 30 metres tall at Morven Park, and a Shumard oak in Sterling.
meta_description: Leesburg, Virginia's remarkable trees, from a white oak older than the 1758 town to the state champion silver linden on the Saint John the Apostle grounds.
question_meta: The oldest tree in Leesburg is the Heritage Tree, a white oak in Ida Lee Park the town puts at well over 250 years. Its story, and the town's other trees.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Leesburg is the Leesburg Heritage Tree, a white oak beside the Rust Farm House in Ida Lee Park, 50 Ida Lee Drive NW. The town's Tree Commission puts it at well over 250 years, grown from seed before Leesburg was founded in 1758. That age is the town's statement rather than a ring count. The next oldest on our map is the Shumard oak in Algonkian Regional Park in Sterling, which Loudoun County estimates at about 200 years.
question_context: Leesburg's trees are better measured than they are dated. Loudoun County's forester keeps a Big Tree Registry and remeasured it in 2025, so the girth, height and crown of every tree on it are recent and on the record. What the registry does not give is ages. The few that exist come from other voices. The town's Tree Commission says its Heritage Tree grew from an acorn before the town was founded, and the county caption for the Shumard oak in Algonkian Regional Park puts it at about 200 years, without saying how either figure was reached. So treat the ages on this page as estimates and the measurements as facts. The best walk is short. On the Saint John the Apostle grounds off Church Street NE, a Japanese chestnut and a shellbark hickory stand seven metres apart, with a silver linden and an Atlantic white cedar, both state champions by the county's list, within about a hundred metres. Ida Lee Park and its Heritage Tree are under a kilometre away; Morven Park is a short drive north-west.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Leesburg?
faq.a: The Leesburg Heritage Tree, a white oak beside the Rust Farm House in Ida Lee Park. The town's Tree Commission says it is well over 250 years old and grew from seed before Leesburg was founded in 1758; no ring count has been published.

Four of Loudoun County's registered big trees stand on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church off Church Street NE, within about a hundred metres of each other. The silver linden there, 246 inches round, is the county's Virginia champion for its species. The Shumard oak in Algonkian Regional Park, 109 feet tall, is the tallest on our Leesburg map.

faq.q: Are Leesburg's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Most are. Ida Lee Park is a free town park, the Morven Park grounds are free to walk from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily, and the county lists the Saint John the Apostle trees as visible from public property, though it is worth checking for services or funerals before walking onto the church grounds. Algonkian Regional Park may charge for parking at busy times. The Oatlands ginkgo, south of town, stands in the ticketed grounds of Oatlands Historic House and Gardens.

faq.q: Can I see Leesburg's trees on foot?
faq.a: The Saint John the Apostle trees and the Heritage Tree in Ida Lee Park are under a kilometre apart in town, and a Loudoun County Transit stop at Union Street and King Street is a few minutes from the church. Morven Park is about 2 km north-west, and Algonkian Regional Park in Sterling is about 25 to 30 minutes east by car.

trees.name: Japanese Chestnut at Saint John the Apostle

location.address: Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church grounds, 101 Oakcrest Manor Dr NE, Leesburg, VA 20176

location_site.name: Saint John the Apostle church grounds and cemetery, Church Street NE

trees.story:
For a while nobody could agree what this tree was. Nominated to Virginia Tech's big-tree database in 2015, it was first listed as a European chestnut. The American Chestnut Foundation took a closer look and concluded it was a Japanese chestnut, partly because it is very old and shows no sign of chestnut blight, the disease that wiped out the American chestnut and that Asian chestnuts largely shrug off.

It grows on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church in Leesburg, just north of a spring house at a sharp turn of Church Street. In 2015 its trunk was 161 inches round. When the Loudoun County forester remeasured it in 2025 it had reached 171 inches, about 4.3 metres, with a height of 54 feet (16.5 metres) and a crown 55 feet across. That is a tree as wide as it is tall.

Whether it is a state champion depends on whom you ask. The county's 2025 list marks it as Virginia's champion Japanese chestnut. The Virginia Tech record says it is not. The two sources disagree, and neither explains why.

It has company. A shellbark hickory stands about seven metres away, and two more county-registered trees, a silver linden and an Atlantic white cedar, are within a hundred metres on the same grounds. No source dates any of them. If you know when the chestnut was planted, or who brought it to Leesburg, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low, wide crown of a chestnut 4.3 metres round, beside a much taller shellbark hickory seven metres away. It stands just north of the spring house at the sharp turn of Church Street.

trees.verify_notes: Virginia Tech Big Tree record 2457 (nominated by Robert Vickers, 2015): Japanese chestnut, 161 in girth, 45 ft, crown 40 ft, status 'legacy', not a Virginia champion; land owner St. John the Apostle Catholic Church; GPS 39.11885,-77.56139; 'just north of a spring house at a sharp turn of Church Street, entering the grounds from the south'. Identification was hard: Virginia Tech first said Castanea sativa; The American Chestnut Foundation concluded Castanea crenata, partly because the tree is 'very aged' and shows no chestnut blight. Loudoun County registry remeasured 2025: 171 in (434 cm), 54 ft (16.5 m), crown 55 ft, marked Virginia champion in the county list (VT record says not champion, conflict between the two, not resolved). Alive: measured 2025 by the county. No age given by any source; left empty. Trees lsb_001 and lsb_004 stand about 7 m apart; lsb_001 to lsb_004 are the four registered trees on this one site. trees.name: Atlantic White Cedar at Saint John the Apostle

location.address: Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church grounds, Church Street NE, Leesburg, VA 20176

location_site.name: Saint John the Apostle church grounds and cemetery, Church Street NE

trees.story:
Virginia's champion Atlantic white cedar does not grow in a swamp. It grows on a church lawn in Leesburg, far inland from the coastal wetlands where its species belongs.

Atlantic white cedar is a tree of the Atlantic coastal plain, a narrow evergreen of bogs and swampy ground along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. This one stands on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church, on Church Street NE, and the Loudoun County Big Tree Registry measured it in 2025 at 58 feet tall (17.7 metres), with a trunk 125 inches round (about 3.2 metres) and a crown only 31 feet across. That slim shape is typical of the species. Its score of 191 points puts it at the top of Virginia's list for its kind, according to the county.

How it got here is a mystery. No source we have found says who planted it or when, and nobody has dated it. A swamp cedar on a Piedmont church lawn was almost certainly planted, and the parish or the town may remember by whom. If you know, tell us.

It is one of four registered trees on these grounds, all within about a hundred metres of each other. The others are a Japanese chestnut, a shellbark hickory and a silver linden that is itself a Virginia champion. The cedar is the evergreen among them, standing about 45 metres east of the chestnut.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the narrow evergreen among the church's big registered trees, about 3.2 metres round and 18 metres tall. It stands about 45 metres east of the Japanese chestnut on the Saint John the Apostle grounds.

trees.name: Silver Linden at Saint John the Apostle

location.address: Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church grounds, Church Street NE, Leesburg, VA 20176

location_site.name: Saint John the Apostle church grounds and cemetery, Church Street NE

trees.story:
The widest trunk on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church belongs to a tree from the other side of the Atlantic. This silver linden measures 246 inches round, about 6.25 metres, and the Loudoun County Big Tree Registry's 2025 list marks it as Virginia's champion of its species.

That is a remarkable girth for any linden. Silver linden is native to south-eastern Europe and western Asia, a tree planted in American towns for its shade and its leaves, dark green above and silvery white beneath, so the crown flickers pale when the wind turns them. The county measured this one at 69 feet tall (21 metres), with a crown 61 feet across, for a total of 330 points. Of the four registered trees on these grounds, it has the widest trunk by a long way. The Japanese chestnut nearby is about 4.3 metres round.

Nobody seems to have written down when it went in. The county gives no age and no planting date, and no other source we know of does. A linden this broad in a churchyard is the kind of tree a parish photograph or a town history might show as a sapling. If you have one, or know the story, tell us.

The tree stands towards the north of the church grounds off Church Street NE, a few minutes' walk from King Street in the middle of town. Check for services or funerals before walking in.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 6.25 metres round, the widest of the four registered trees on the grounds, and by leaves silvery white underneath. It stands towards the north of the Saint John the Apostle grounds.

trees.name: Shellbark Hickory at Saint John the Apostle

location.address: Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church grounds, Church Street NE, Leesburg, VA 20176

location_site.name: Saint John the Apostle church grounds and cemetery, Church Street NE

trees.story:
Seven metres apart on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church stand two trees that could hardly be built more differently. One is a Japanese chestnut, short and broad. The other is this shellbark hickory, and at 98 feet (29.9 metres) it is almost twice as tall, the tallest of the four county-registered trees on the site.

The Loudoun County Big Tree Registry's 2025 measurements give it a trunk 113 inches round, about 2.9 metres, and a crown 73 feet across, for 229 points. It is not a state champion, and it does not need to be. Shellbark hickory is a native of river bottoms and rich lowland woods in the eastern United States, known for the largest nuts of any hickory and for bark that comes away in long, loose plates.

Together with the chestnut it makes one stop, and you can stand between the two and see both. The silver linden and the Atlantic white cedar complete the set within about a hundred metres.

No source gives this hickory an age or a planting date, and nobody seems to know whether it was planted at all. If you know, tell us. Check for services or funerals before walking onto the grounds.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 30 metres, twice that of the broad Japanese chestnut seven metres away. It stands near the sharp turn of Church Street on the Saint John the Apostle grounds.

trees.name: Tulip Poplar at Morven Park

location.address: Morven Park, 17195 Southern Planter Lane, Leesburg, VA 20176 (near the Westmoreland Davis mansion)

trees.story:
Ninety-seven feet is about the height of a nine-storey building, and that is how tall the Loudoun County Big Tree Registry measured this tulip tree near the mansion at Morven Park in 2025. In metres, 29.6. Its trunk is 154 inches round, about 3.9 metres, and its crown spreads 68 feet, for a total of 268 points.

Morven Park is a thousand-acre estate on the north-western edge of Leesburg, once the home of Westmoreland Davis, the Virginia governor who bought it in 1903. His wife Marguerite laid out the formal boxwood gardens in 1930. Mansion tours are ticketed, but the grounds are free to walk every day from seven in the morning until six in the evening.

What the paperwork does not tell us is how old the tree is. The Davises' arrival in 1903 and the 1930 gardens date the estate's later history, not this trunk, and no source we have seen gives a planting date or an age. A tulip tree this size could predate both, or not. Nobody knows. If you do, tell us.

The county's pin places the tree in the mansion area, but on an estate this size it is approximate, so look for a big tulip tree near the house rather than trusting the dot to the metre. Tulip trees are easy to tell apart from the rest by their square-ended leaves, shaped like the outline of a tulip.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, square-ended like a tulip's outline, on a trunk about 3.9 metres round and nearly 30 metres tall. It stands near the Westmoreland Davis mansion; the county's pin is approximate.

trees.name: Oatlands Ginkgo
trees.age_estimate: close to 200 years, by the estate's arborist

location.address: Oatlands Historic House and Gardens, 20850 Oatlands Plantation Lane, Leesburg, VA 20175

trees.story:
The man who looks after Oatlands' trees calls this the third largest ginkgo in the United States. The Loudoun County Big Tree Registry's 2025 measurements make the claim easy to believe, with 103 feet in height (31.4 metres), a trunk 201 inches round (about 5.1 metres), and a crown 69 feet across, for 321 points.

It grows behind the mansion at Oatlands, a historic house and garden south of Leesburg on Route 15. Jim Donegan, the estate's tree contractor, told Middleburg Life it is close to 200 years old. That is an arborist's estimate, and no ring count or planting record has been published to back it, so it stands as his judgement rather than a date. The national ranking is his too.

The ginkgo is the only living species of a lineage older than the dinosaurs, and it shrugs off pests and pollution in a way that has made it a favourite of city streets. This one has had room and time instead. Its neighbours at Oatlands include an American boxwood canopy and yews the same article puts at around 200 years.

In November the whole crown turns butter yellow and then drops in a day or two, which is the moment to come. The gardens and grounds are open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. with a ticket. The county's 2025 measurement is the latest record of it; if you have seen it since, tell us it still stands.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped leaves on a trunk about 5.1 metres round and over 30 metres tall. It stands behind the Oatlands mansion, inside the ticketed grounds.

official_register.name: Loudoun County Big Tree Registry (Dept of Building & Development, Forest Resources; measured 2025)

trees.access: Oatlands gardens and grounds open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily with a ticket (Oatlands plan-your-visit page); the ginkgo stands behind the mansion, so it is inside the paid grounds.
trees.transport: 5 miles south of downtown Leesburg on Route 15, about a 12 minute drive. No public transport found.

best_time.label: November, when the whole crown turns butter yellow and drops within days

trees.name: Leesburg Heritage Tree
trees.age_estimate: well over 250 years, by the town

location.address: Ida Lee Park, beside the Rust Farm House, 50 Ida Lee Drive NW, Leesburg, VA 20176

location_site.name: Rust Farm House yard, Ida Lee Park

trees.story:
Leesburg's own Tree Commission says this white oak grew from an acorn before there was a Leesburg. The town was founded in 1758, and the commission's Tree Walk of Historic Leesburg calls its Heritage Tree a fine specimen of white oak well over 250 years old.

It stands in Ida Lee Park, next to the Rust Farm House, a farmhouse from around 1859 at 50 Ida Lee Drive NW. If the town's figure is right, the oak was about a century old when the house went up beside it. The farmhouse now stands by the park's festival field.

Take the age as the town's statement. The leaflet gives no ring count or measurement behind it, and we have found no published girth for the tree. The town's own America 250 page adds that the park once held several mature white oaks, and in May 2026 the town planted a Mount Vernon chestnut oak sapling beside the farmhouse. That sapling is not the Heritage Tree, so look past it for the old trunk.

One more honest caveat. The leaflet is undated, and nobody we can cite has confirmed the oak since. A local newspaper reported in January 2026 that the town's tree inventory had measured a massive white oak in Ida Lee Park, which may or may not be this one. If you have been to the farmhouse lately, or know its girth, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big old white oak beside the Rust Farm House, not the young chestnut oak planted there in May 2026. It stands in Ida Lee Park next to the farmhouse at 50 Ida Lee Drive NW.
trees.access: Ida Lee Park is a free town park. The tree is next to the Rust Farm House beside the festival field.
trees.transport: About 1.2 km north-west of downtown Leesburg; roughly 15 minutes on foot. No bus checked.
trees.verify_notes: Source: the Town of Leesburg Tree Commission's 'Tree Walk of Historic Leesburg' leaflet (read through a Wayback copy): 'Leesburg Heritage Tree' is 'a fine specimen of a Northern White Oak that is well over 250 years old and grew from a seed before the Town of Leesburg was founded in 1758'; located 'next to Rust Farm House, circa 1859 (50 Ida Lee Drive NW)'. Age is the town's statement, no core or measurement cited. Pin is the farmhouse address point (39.12406,-77.56477, Nominatim/OSM), not the trunk; no tree node with species in OSM; no girth. The town's America 250 page says the park 'once' had several mature white oaks and planted a Mount Vernon chestnut oak sapling beside the farmhouse in May 2026 (do not confuse the sapling with the heritage oak). A Loudoun Times piece of 23 Jan 2026 reports the town's tree inventory measuring a 'massive white oak' at Ida Lee Park (arborist Jack Myrna; article text paywalled, not read, not necessarily the same tree). Alive: not confirmed since the leaflet (leaflet undated, archive copy Jan 2026); the 2026 article suggests a large white oak stands there. Flagged: single source, pin is a site.

trees.name: Shumard Oak at Algonkian Regional Park

location.address: Algonkian Regional Park, Sterling, VA (NOVA Parks), off the park's trail network near Sugarland Run

trees.story:
Loudoun County counts this Shumard oak among the largest trees in the whole county, and it stands not in a town square but out on the trails of Algonkian Regional Park, near Sugarland Run in Sterling. The county's caption gives it as 109 feet high, 184 inches round the trunk and about 200 years old.

The 2025 registry figures put numbers on the rest. The trunk is about 4.7 metres round, the tree 33.2 metres tall, and the crown spreads 83 feet, for 313.75 points. An older figure, quoted by The Nature Conservancy's Virginia public lands page, gave it 112 feet and 176 inches. Measurements drift between surveys, and the county's are the latest.

Shumard oak is a red oak of southern bottomlands and stream banks, a big, fast tree with deeply cut, bristle-tipped leaves. The 200-year figure is the county's estimate, and it does not say how it was reached, so treat it as a forester's judgement rather than a date. If it holds, the oak was a sapling in the early 1800s.

This is the far outlier on the Leesburg page. Sterling is about 20 kilometres east of downtown, 25 to 30 minutes by car on Route 7, with no useful bus. Algonkian is a NOVA Parks park and may charge for parking at busy times, so check before you go.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, a Shumard oak about 4.7 metres round and 33 metres tall, with bristle-tipped oak leaves. It stands just off the trails of Algonkian Regional Park near Sugarland Run; the county pin is approximate.

trees.name: The Red Mulberry of the W&OD Trail

location.address: W&OD Trail bridle path, Washington & Old Dominion Railroad Regional Park, Ashburn, VA

trees.story:
Only five of the 32 trees on Loudoun County's Big Tree Registry have a thicker trunk than this red mulberry, and three of those five are sycamores more than twice its height. The mulberry is 218 inches round, about 5.5 metres, but only 45 feet tall, about 14 metres, with a crown some 13 metres across. The county measured all three in 2025.

It grows beside the bridle trail of the Washington and Old Dominion Railroad Regional Park in Ashburn. NOVA Parks runs the park along the former roadbed of the W&OD Railroad, a paved trail of 45 miles between Shirlington and Purcellville, with a 32-mile gravel horse trail beside it for riders.

The registry ranks trees on points, trunk inches plus height in feet plus a quarter of the crown, and height is where the mulberry loses ground. It scores 273.5, well behind the tall sycamores. On girth alone it beats the Shumard oak in Algonkian Regional Park, 33 metres tall, which the county calls one of the largest trees in Loudoun.

It is not marked as a Virginia champion. The county flags it as visible or accessible from public property, which on a public trail is the easy part.

Nobody has published an age for it. If you know how long it has stood here, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 5.5 metres round, on a mulberry only about 14 metres tall with a crown some 13 metres across. It stands beside the gravel bridle trail of the W&OD Trail in Ashburn.

official_register.name: Loudoun County Big Tree Registry (Dept of Building & Development, Forest Resources; measured 2025)

trees.access: Free. On the Washington & Old Dominion Railroad Regional Park (NOVA Parks), beside the gravel horse trail that runs next to the paved W&OD Trail. The county flags this tree as visible or accessible from public property.
trees.transport: Ashburn, about 10 km south-east of downtown Leesburg in a straight line, on the W&OD Trail itself, so you can cycle or walk the trail from Leesburg. No public transport verified.
